adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache serves stale denies after permissions are granted because existing invalidation logic doesn't cover the new permDenialCache keys, creating a stale-authorization window until shortCacheTTL expires

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new negative-cache `permDenialCache` that is checked first in `Service.Check` and immediately returns `Allowed: false` if the key exists (service.go: `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). The cache is populated on any computed deny (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). There is no code in the diff that ever deletes/invalidates these deny entries when permissions change, so a prior denial will continue to override later-granted permissions until `shortCacheTTL` expires, creating a stale-authorization (stale-deny) window. This behavior is directly implied by the new short-circuit logic even without referencing any external invalidation mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: userPermDenialCacheKey joins action, name, and parent with unescaped underscores, allowing key collisions between resources whose UIDs contain underscores, causing incorrect denies with no fallback
Swallowed errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions in Check: real DB errors are silently discarded, causing the failed identifier lookup to execute twice per request with no log on the first failure

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the result of getCachedIdentityPermissions is only used when err == nil; any non-nil error is ignored and execution falls through to s.getIdentityPermissions (new code around `cachedPerms, err := ...` and subsequent `permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)`). Since getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors (it calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` for user/service-account types and returns that error), those errors are effectively treated like a cache miss with no log/handling at that point. This can also cause `GetUserIdentifiers` to be invoked twice in one request (once in getCachedIdentityPermissions, again in getIdentityPermissions/getUserPermissions). This is a concrete, diff-grounded concern, but it’s primarily efficiency/observability rather than a demonstrable correctness break from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage metric is incremented unconditionally with 'false' after the cached-permissions block, conflating cache hit/miss with allow/deny outcome when the cache hit but permission check returned false

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, after calling getCachedIdentityPermissions, the code only increments permissionCacheUsage with "true" when the cached permission check results in Allowed==true (or when permDenialCache hits). If cached permissions are present but checkPermission returns false (e.g., cache is outdated/doesn’t include the specific resource), execution falls through and then unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage with "false" before querying the DB. This makes the metric reflect “cache led to an allow/deny decision” rather than “cache hit/miss”, which can undercount cache hits and effectively ties the "true" label to allow outcomes. This is a metrics/observability semantics issue, not a functional correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Stale denial cache (permDenialCache) has no invalidation path when user permissions change, so a newly granted user can still be denied until TTL expiry

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a negative cache `permDenialCache` that short-circuits authorization: in `Service.Check`, if `permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits, the method immediately returns `Allowed: false` without re-checking current permissions (`return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil`). Denials are stored on any `!allowed` outcome (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`). The diff shows no invalidation mechanism tied to permission changes (only TTL via `newCacheWrap(..., shortCacheTTL)`), so a user who is granted permission shortly after a cached denial can continue to be denied until the TTL expires.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache key uses raw request UserUID while the permission cache uses resolved userIdentifiers.UID, causing asymmetry that can pin denials to a caller-controlled key component

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the denial cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.UserUID, ...)`), but permission caching (and cached lookup) canonicalizes the user identifier via `GetUserIdentifiers(...)` and then uses `userIdentifiers.UID` to form keys (`userPermCacheKey(ns.Value, userIdentifiers.UID, action)` in `getCachedIdentityPermissions`). This asymmetry is directly visible in the diff and can cause incorrect caching behavior if `checkReq.UserUID` is not already the canonical UID (e.g., alternate representations/aliases), allowing denials to be stored/looked up under a different key than the one used for permission evaluation, potentially enabling denial bypass or denial pinning under caller-influenced key material.

adjudication_records.issue_text: NoopCache used by the in-process rbacClient silently drops cache invalidations (Delete is a no-op), potentially delaying permission revocation propagation

adjudication.rationale: In `ProvideAuthZClient`, the in-process `rbacClient` is constructed with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})`. That `NoopCache` implementation makes **all reads miss** (`Get` returns `cache.ErrNotFound`) and **all writes no-op** (`Set` returns nil), so the client effectively has *no caching at all*. While `Delete` is also a no-op, there is nothing stored to invalidate, so the diff does not support the claim that this would delay permission revocation propagation due to dropped invalidations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Metrics misattribution/double-counting: cache-hit metrics can be misleading when denial cache hits are reported after fallthrough miscounting

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, cache usage metrics are potentially misleading: (1) a denial-cache hit (`permDenialCache.Get(...)`) increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"true"` even though it’s not a permission-cache hit (it’s a separate negative cache), and (2) when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached perms but `checkPermission` yields `allowed == false`, the code falls through to DB and then increments `permissionCacheUsage` as `"false"` (miss) after the `if err == nil { ... }` block, even though the cache lookup itself was a hit. This is misattribution rather than functional breakage; no clear double-counting is shown because each path increments at most once before returning or proceeding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative (denial) cache has no invalidation path, so users can be denied after permissions are granted until TTL expiry

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new negative cache is treated as authoritative: if `permDenialCache.Get(ctx, permDenialKey)` returns ok, the handler immediately returns `Allowed: false` without consulting the permission store (`return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil`). The denial entry is created whenever a DB-backed check results in `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`), and the diff shows no invalidation/delete path when permissions change. Therefore, after a permission grant, a previously cached denial can incorrectly keep denying until the cache TTL expires.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache has one entry per (user, action, resource name, folder), causing write amplification and unbounded key growth on the cache backend

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new denial cache keyed by `namespace`, `userUID`, `action`, `name`, and `parent` via `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` (pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go). In `Service.Check`, on any non-allowed result it writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` (pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go), and it checks this key on subsequent requests to short-circuit to deny. This does create potentially very high-cardinality keys (per resource name/folder) and will write on every deny, which can amplify cache writes and key count. However, the keys are stored with `shortCacheTTL` (see `newCacheWrap[bool](..., shortCacheTTL)`), so growth is time-bounded rather than strictly unbounded; still, the high cardinality/write volume concern is real and diff-grounded but not a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ProvideAuthZClient now uses NoopCache instead of a 30s local cache, increasing RPCs to the authz server

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ProvideAuthZClient` switching from `rbacClient := newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(channel, authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, and `NoopCache.Get` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`. Meanwhile, the 30s `cache.NewLocalCache(...)` remains only in `newRemoteRBACClient`. So for the in-process client created in `ProvideAuthZClient`, client-side caching is effectively disabled, which would increase request volume over that client interface (more RPC-style calls through the gRPC channel) compared to a local cache. This is a performance/architecture concern, not a correctness defect, based on the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage metric double-counts or misattributes hits in the fallback path where a cache hit that didn't authorize is reported as a miss

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, a successful cache lookup (err == nil from getCachedIdentityPermissions) that results in allowed == false falls through and increments `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", action)` (the miss path). That means a real cache hit is recorded as a miss whenever cached perms don’t authorize and the code falls back to DB, so the metric is misattributed in this fallback path (though it is not actually double-counted in this code).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache is checked first in Check and never invalidated when permissions are granted (role change), causing newly granted permissions to remain denied up to shortCacheTTL (60s)

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted before any permission evaluation (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The cache is populated on a deny (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`) and there is no code path that clears/invalidates this denial entry when permissions later become allowed (e.g., role/permission changes), nor is it overridden by a subsequent allow because the denial check happens first. This means a previously denied (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) check can remain denied until the cache entry expires (shortCacheTTL), even if permissions are granted in the meantime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: userPermDenialCacheKey collides byte-for-byte with userPermCacheKey when Name/ParentFolder are empty, causing cache corruption between wrappers that deserialize different types (bool vs map[string]bool)

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `userPermCacheKey(namespace,userUID,action)` returns `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action`, while `userPermDenialCacheKey(..., name, parent)` always appends two additional separators: `"_" + name + "_" + parent`. Even when `name` and `parent` are empty strings, the denial key becomes `... + action + "__"`, which is not byte-for-byte equal to the permission key (`... + action`). Therefore the claimed cache-key collision (and resulting type deserialization corruption between `*cacheWrap[bool]` and `*cacheWrap[map[string]bool]`) is not supported by the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions can return non-ErrNotFound errors for TypeUser which Check silently masks, treating DB errors as cache misses without logging

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the result of `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` is only used when `err == nil`; any non-nil error (including non-`cache.ErrNotFound` errors returned by `getCachedIdentityPermissions` for `TypeUser` via `GetUserIdentifiers`) is ignored and treated the same as a cache miss (no log/metric distinguishing error vs miss) before falling back to `getIdentityPermissions`. This is a real observability/behavior nuance introduced by the change, but it’s not clearly a correctness bug because the DB fallback still runs and will log/return an error if the underlying DB call fails there too.

adjudication_records.issue_text: List metric semantics drift: permissionCacheUsage hit/miss label distribution changes and per-identity-type spans/metrics disappear on cache hits compared to old instrumentation

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves cache-hit/miss accounting for List from deeper calls (previously in getUserPermissions; anonymous had no cache metric at all) to the top of Service.List: it now increments permissionCacheUsage based solely on getCachedIdentityPermissions success/failure. On cache hits, List returns without calling getIdentityPermissions (and thus without executing spans/logic in getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions), so prior per-path spans/metrics won’t appear on hits. This is a semantics change in instrumentation rather than a functional correctness bug, but it can affect metric dashboards/alerts relying on the old behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache is never invalidated on permission changes, causing stale denials after grants since denial check runs before perm-cache/DB check and invalidation logic only clears userPermCacheKey

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `permDenialCache` and makes it a hard deny fast-path in `Service.Check`: it computes `permDenialKey` and if present immediately returns `Allowed: false` before checking cached permissions or fetching from the DB (service.go: new block at start of `Check`). The only write to this cache is `s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` when `!allowed` after a DB-backed check, and there is no corresponding deletion/clearing logic shown in this diff—only TTL-based expiry via `newCacheWrap(..., shortCacheTTL)`. This means a permission grant/change can be masked until the denial entry expires, because the denial cache overrides both the permission cache and the DB check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unbounded cardinality of denial cache keys since keys embed name and parent, causing memory growth under deny-heavy traffic with many distinct resource names

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new denial cache keyed by `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` (`userPermDenialCacheKey` in `cache.go`) and populates it on every denied `Check` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` in `service.go`). Because the key embeds `name` and `parent`, the number of distinct keys can grow with the number of distinct resources/folders requested, and there is no bound/eviction policy shown beyond TTL (`newCacheWrap[bool](cache, ..., shortCacheTTL)`). This is a diff-grounded scalability/memory-pressure concern under deny-heavy traffic, not a direct correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Folder-parameter asymmetry: denial cache includes ParentFolder but requests may or may not include it, causing cache misses and inconsistent denial/allow decisions on variants of the same request

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial-cache key is built with `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)`), so the same user/action/name will map to different cache entries depending on whether `ParentFolder` is empty vs populated. The diff does not show how `ParentFolder` is derived from the incoming `authzv1.CheckRequest` (which in tests uses `Folder`), so it’s not verifiable that callers “may or may not include it” for semantically identical checks. But the cache-key sensitivity to folder presence is real and could lead to inconsistent cache behavior across request variants.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels cache-hit-denied decisions as cache misses, distorting cache-hit-rate metrics

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, when getCachedIdentityPermissions returns successfully (cache hit) but checkPermission yields allowed==false, the code falls through and unconditionally increments `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action)` (the line after the `if err == nil { ... }` block). This records a cache miss even though the permission cache was hit; only cache-hit allows (and the separate `permDenialCache` hit path) are labeled as hits. That verifiably distorts the cache-hit-rate metric for deny outcomes based on cached permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Check silently swallows errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions for user identities, causing double-fetch and invisible identifier-store failures with no log/metric

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the result of `getCachedIdentityPermissions` is only used when `err == nil`; any non-nil error is ignored and the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` without logging/metrics (`cachedPerms, err := ...; if err == nil { ... } ... permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)`). In `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, the user/service-account path calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` and can return a real error (not just `cache.ErrNotFound`), which will be silently treated like a cache miss and retried via `getIdentityPermissions` (potentially double-fetching identifiers and hiding transient identifier-store errors). This is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/efficiency issue, but it doesn’t clearly change correctness since the later DB path will still error/log if it fails again.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test setup uses fixed TTLs and no test exercises denial cache TTL expiry or invalidation, leaving the stale-denial failure mode untested

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new negative-result cache (Service.permDenialCache) that is populated on denial in Check() (s.permDenialCache.Set(...)) and short-circuits future checks when present (if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }). Tests add coverage for the presence of an explicit deny entry ("Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"), but none exercise expiry/invalidation of this denial cache entry. The test setup uses a real local cache with fixed expiry/cleanup intervals in setupService() (cache.NewLocalCache(...Expiry: 5 * time.Minute...)) and wraps permDenialCache with shortCacheTTL, yet no test advances time or verifies the denial entry eventually disappears, leaving the stale-denial behavior untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test that the denial cache (permDenialCache) is invalidated when a user's permissions change, and no grant-side invalidation hook exists — stale denials can persist up to shortCacheTTL

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a negative-result cache `permDenialCache` that is checked before consulting cached perms or the DB (`Service.Check`: early return `Allowed: false` if `permDenialCache.Get` hits) and is populated on any denied check (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). There is no corresponding invalidation/clearing logic on subsequent grants/permission changes in this diff, so a previously denied (namespace,userUID,action,name,parentFolder) tuple will continue to force denial until the cache entry expires (constructed with `newCacheWrap[bool](..., shortCacheTTL)`). Tests added cover the deny cache hit case, but do not cover behavior when permissions change (e.g., denial entry should be cleared or bypassed). This is a concrete review concern introduced by the new denial cache behavior, but it’s not provably a defect without knowing the intended caching semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache key built by joining userUID, action, name, parent with '_' has no delimiter safety, causing collisions between distinct (name, folder) pairs that cross-contaminate denials
Deleted cache-hit test in getUserPermissions was not replaced with equivalent coverage verifying permCache is actually populated after a DB fallback

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the explicit cache-hit test case from `TestService_getUserPermissions` (the test verifying returning permissions from `permCache`), and the new tests added (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only verify (a) allow from cached perms, and (b) fallback to DB on cache miss/outdated cache. None of the new coverage asserts that after a DB fallback (e.g., `s.getIdentityPermissions` path in `Check` / `List`), the resulting permissions are written back into `s.permCache`. Given the refactor that moved cache reads into `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and removed cache reads from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, adding a test that the DB path populates `permCache` would be a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage, but not a demonstrated functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The denial-cache write path (deny → cache populated → second Check short-circuits) is untested; the permDenialCache.Set on denial is never executed by any test

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new write-on-deny behavior in Service.Check: `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` and a new read short-circuit at the top of Check that denies if the key exists. The newly added tests in `TestService_CacheCheck` only cover the read path by pre-populating `permDenialCache` ("Should deny on explicit cache deny entry") and do not create a denial via `Check` that would trigger the new `permDenialCache.Set` write path, nor do they validate that a first denial causes a second Check to short-circuit. However, the stronger claim that `permDenialCache.Set` is "never executed by any test" cannot be proven from the diff alone because existing (unchanged) tests may already exercise a denial path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test coverage for anonymous and render-service identities in the new Check fast paths, including anonymous denial-cache key collisions across anonymous callers

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new “fast path” logic in `Service.Check` that first consults `permDenialCache` (via `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`) and then `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` before falling back to DB (`getIdentityPermissions`). The added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`) cover only the user/UID case; they do not cover `types.TypeAnonymous` or `types.TypeRenderService` branches in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (which returns `cache.ErrNotFound` for render-service and uses `anonymousPermCacheKey` for anonymous). Also, `permDenialKey` is computed unconditionally from `checkReq.UserUID`/`Action`/`Name`/`ParentFolder` before identity-type branching, so anonymous/render-service behavior (including what happens when `UserUID` is empty and keys potentially collide) is not exercised by tests in this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: List cache-hit test lacks negative coverage for denied/empty lists and non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions, which are silently swallowed as cache misses

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.List`, the new cache path treats **any** error from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` as a cache miss (`if err == nil { ... } else { ... permissions, err = s.getIdentityPermissions(...) }`), so errors other than `cache.ErrNotFound` (e.g., `GetUserIdentifiers` failure or `unsupported identity type` from `getCachedIdentityPermissions`) are not surfaced from the cache attempt and will be effectively ignored if the DB path succeeds. The added `TestService_CacheList` only asserts the positive cache-hit case and does not cover empty/denied results or the non-`ErrNotFound` error path behavior introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test assertions for the changed permissionCacheUsage metrics semantics, leaving the behavioral change affecting dashboards/alerting unverified

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes where/how `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented: it was previously updated inside `getUserPermissions` (and implicitly for anonymous in `getAnonymousPermissions`), but now it’s updated in `Service.Check` and `Service.List`, with new semantics (e.g., in `Check`, a cached permissions map that doesn’t grant access falls through and is counted as `WithLabelValues("false", action)` even though the cache was hit). New tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) exercise cache behavior but contain no assertions on `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage` counters, so this behavioral/metrics change is unverified by tests in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative-denial cache entries (permDenialCache) have no invalidation path; existing invalidation logic targets the older userPermCacheKey format, so denials persist up to shortCacheTTL after a permission is granted, and the two near-identical key builders risk invalidation sites missing one

adjudication.rationale:
The diff introduces `permDenialCache` as a negative-result cache that is consulted first in `Service.Check`:
- It short-circuits to `Allowed: false` if `permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits (service.go `Check`, new `permDenialKey` block).
- On any computed denial, it stores `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`.
In the shown code, there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation for `permDenialCache` entries, and its key (`userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`) is distinct from the existing positive permission cache key (`userPermCacheKey(...)`). That means any invalidation logic that only clears the old permission cache key (not shown here, but implied by the split) would not clear denial entries, so a previously-denied check can remain denied until `shortCacheTTL` even after permissions are granted. This is a correctness issue introduced by the new early-return denial cache behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cache-check responsibility was moved into callers via getCachedIdentityPermissions; any caller of getIdentityPermissions directly gets no caching or cache metrics, with the read-through concern living as a caller-side precondition

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes cache-read and cache-metrics from the underlying permission fetch paths (e.g., in getUserPermissions the `permCache.Get(...)` short-circuit and `permissionCacheUsage` increments were deleted; similarly in getAnonymousPermissions the cache get was removed). Cache reads are now performed only by the new caller-side helper `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, which is used in `Service.Check` and `Service.List`. Therefore, any other (current or future) caller that invokes `getIdentityPermissions` directly will not benefit from cache reads (and will miss cache-usage metrics), making caching a caller-side precondition. However, the finding overstates slightly by saying such callers get "no caching" at all—`getIdentityPermissions` still appears to populate caches downstream—so this is primarily an architectural/performance concern rather than a correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache is consulted using raw checkReq.UserUID/Namespace before GetUserIdentifiers resolution, while userPermCacheKey uses the resolved identity — two caches use different identity domains for the same subject

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` key is built from `checkReq.Namespace.Value` + raw `checkReq.UserUID` before any `GetUserIdentifiers` resolution (`permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.UserUID, ...)`). By contrast, permission caching for users/service accounts in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` uses `GetUserIdentifiers(..., userID)` and then keys `permCache` by `userIdentifiers.UID` (`userPermCacheKey(ns.Value, userIdentifiers.UID, action)`). This is a real inconsistency in identity domains between the two caches, which can reduce cache hit rates / make behavior dependent on which identifier form is used, but the diff alone doesn’t prove it causes incorrect authorization decisions (a miss just falls back to DB), so it’s not a clearly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions conflates cache misses, unsupported identity types, and store errors in a single error return; callers swallow all errors as misses, and the duplicated switch logic in getIdentityPermissions will drift

adjudication.rationale: In `Check` and `List`, the code treats any non-nil error from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` as a cache miss and falls back to `getIdentityPermissions` (see `if err == nil { ... } else { ... permissions, err = s.getIdentityPermissions(...) }`). This does conflate `cache.ErrNotFound` with other errors (e.g., `GetUserIdentifiers` failures or `unsupported identity type`), but those non-cache errors are not ultimately swallowed: the fallback path will typically reproduce and return the error from `getIdentityPermissions`. The main concrete issue shown by the diff is architectural/maintainability: `getCachedIdentityPermissions` duplicates the identity-type switch logic that already exists in `getIdentityPermissions`, increasing drift risk and potentially causing extra work (e.g., calling `GetUserIdentifiers` twice on error paths).

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage 'false' is incremented even when failure was a real identity-store error, corrupting cache-hit-rate metrics during store outages

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...)` is incremented unconditionally whenever `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` returns any error (not just `cache.ErrNotFound`) because the code falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage...Inc()` right after the `if err == nil { ... }` block. But `getCachedIdentityPermissions` can return real errors (e.g., `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` failure), so identity-store outages/errors would be counted as cache misses. The same pattern exists in `Service.List`, where any error from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` increments the "false" label before attempting `getIdentityPermissions` (which may also fail). This is a real, diff-grounded metrics/observability issue, not a functional correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: NoopCache is a generic reusable type defined in the gRPC client-wiring file (rbac.go) with misleading receiver name 'lc', instead of belonging in the cache package, inviting duplication

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `type NoopCache struct{}` and its `Get/Set/Delete` methods at the bottom of `pkg/services/authz/rbac.go`, which is primarily a client/server wiring file. This is a reusable cache implementation (always miss) and the finding’s point that it arguably belongs in a cache-related package/module (to avoid duplication across callers) is grounded in what’s shown. The receiver name `lc` is also a minor readability/style issue visible in the added methods.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Duplicated try-cache → on-miss-fallback-to-DB block between Check and List with inconsistent error logging; should be extracted into a shared helper

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a similar “try cached permissions, otherwise fall back to getIdentityPermissions” pattern in both `Service.Check` (new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` call starting at `permDenialKey := ...` / `cachedPerms, err := ...`) and `Service.List` (new `permissions, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions...` with an `else` falling back to `s.getIdentityPermissions`). This is duplicated logic that could reasonably be extracted into a shared helper. The claim about “inconsistent error logging” is only weakly supported: both paths log DB fetch failures similarly, and cache-miss isn’t logged in either; however the two functions do have slightly different handling/logging around subsequent permission evaluation (`Check` logs on `checkPermission` error while `List` doesn’t have an equivalent step). Overall this is a maintainability concern grounded in the diff, not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache (permDenialCache) is never invalidated on permission changes, so a user granted access after a denial stays denied for up to shortCacheTTL because existing invalidation deletes old userPermCacheKey format keys that don't match the new denial key suffix

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a hit in `permDenialCache` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`) immediately returns `Allowed: false` without consulting `permCache` or the DB (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). The cache entry is written whenever a DB-backed check denies (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). The diff shows no mechanism to clear/update these denial entries when permissions change or when a subsequent check would allow, so a user who is later granted access can remain denied until `shortCacheTTL` expires. The finding’s claim about “existing invalidation deletes old userPermCacheKey format keys” isn’t shown in this diff, but the core stale-deny behavior is verifiable from the added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache keys are collision-prone: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates components with underscores, so names containing underscores (e.g. ("act","a_b","") vs ("act","a","b")) can produce identical keys, causing a denial for one resource to apply to a different resource
matched_golden_ids: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same underlying problem: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds cache keys by concatenating components with underscores, which can be ambiguous when components contain underscores or are empty, leading to key collisions and incorrect denial cache hits affecting permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache hit skips permission evaluation entirely (checked before identity resolution) and there is no code path that deletes a denial entry, so stale or malformed denial entries are trusted unconditionally for the full TTL

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and, on a hit, returns `Allowed: false` immediately (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). This bypasses all further permission evaluation (including the DB fallback used when cached perms are missing/outdated). The only write path shown is `s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` when `!allowed`, and there is no code path in the diff that deletes or invalidates a denial entry aside from TTL expiry. This makes denials “sticky” for the full TTL even if permissions change to allow, unlike the positive-permission cache which falls back to DB on non-allow results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ProvideAuthZClient in rbac.go now uses NoopCache instead of newRBACClient's 30s local cache for the embedded-server path, removing a caching layer and potentially causing latency/throughput regression

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ProvideAuthZClient (embedded-server path) changed from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(channel, authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)` (rbac.go around the first hunk). In contrast, the remote client path still constructs a client with a 30s `cache.NewLocalCache(...)` (newRemoteRBACClient now inlines the previous newRBACClient behavior). This is a real, diff-grounded change that removes client-side caching only for the embedded path and could plausibly cause performance regression, but it is not a correctness defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Metrics are wrong on the fallback path: permissionCacheUsage("false") is incremented when the permission cache was hit (miss was at resource level), and a denial-cache hit is counted as permissionCacheUsage("true"), conflating two different caches

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial-cache hit (`permDenialCache.Get`) increments `metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", ...)` even though this is not a permission-cache hit, conflating two different caches. Also, when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns cached permissions (i.e., permCache hit) but `checkPermission` yields `allowed == false`, the code falls through and later increments `permissionCacheUsage` with `"false"` unconditionally (`s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...).Inc()`), so the metric reports a cache miss despite having used cached permissions (the miss/insufficiency is at the resource/scope level, not the cache level). Both issues are directly visible in the added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cached-allow short-circuit bypasses singleflight freshness coordination: Check trusts cached perms on the allow path without sf.Do while the deny path does a fresh DB read, allowing inconsistent staleness between allow and deny decisions that compounds the denial-cache invalidation issue
matched_golden_ids: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same asymmetric cache-handling behavior: cached allows are trusted and returned immediately (even bypassing coordination), while denies trigger a fresh DB read. This matches the golden issue of trusting stale cached grants while not trusting cached denials, creating inconsistent staleness and potential unauthorized access after revocation.
